---
title: "Quiz: simulation envelopes and global tests"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

---

**Q1.** To test an observed $L(r) - r$ against CSR by simulation, what must the simulated patterns have in common with the observed one?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Four things.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The same number of points, the same window (tissue mask), and the curve must be computed the same way (same function, same edge correction, same radii).
:::

---

**Q2.** The observed L(5) − 5 is larger than 97 of 99 simulated values and smaller than 2. What is the one-sided Monte Carlo p-value?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Count the observed itself.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$(1 + 2)/(1 + 99) = 0.03$.
:::

---

**Q3.** Why can a curve that leaves a 39-simulation pointwise envelope at one of 25 radii not be called significant at 5 %?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How many tests were made?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The 5 % holds for one pre-chosen r. Looking at 25 radii is 25 tests; the chance that a random pattern leaves the band somewhere is much higher (about 37 % in the simulations of the lecture).
:::

---

**Q4.** How does the MAD test avoid the problem?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
One number per curve.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It reduces every curve (observed and simulated) to one number, the largest absolute deviation from the CSR curve over a range of r fixed in advance, and ranks the observed number among the simulated ones: a single test with the right level.
:::

---

**Q5.** A colleague widens the r range, changes from L to g and from 39 to 99 simulations until p < 0.05. What is wrong?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Recall tuning on the test set.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Each choice is another test; picking the one that "works" inflates the false positive rate, exactly like tuning a classifier on its test set. Fix function, range, correction and number of simulations before looking.
:::

---

**Q6.** Is the grey pointwise envelope a confidence band for the observed curve?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What was simulated?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
No. It shows how curves of CSR patterns vary: it describes the null hypothesis. The uncertainty of the observed curve itself needs replicate images (or resampling of images).
:::

---

**Q7.** Three experiments, two conditions, five images each, 200 cells per image. What is n for the comparison of the conditions, and what goes into the test?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Unit of replication.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
n = 3 experiments per condition. Compute one summary per image (e.g. L(r₀) − r₀ at a pre-chosen r₀), average the 5 images of each experiment and condition, and test the 3 vs 3 experiment means (paired by experiment if both conditions were run in each).
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* Why is the rank of the observed statistic among $s$ simulations uniform under the null hypothesis?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Exchangeability.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Under $H_0$ the observed pattern is one more draw from the same process, so $T_0, \dots, T_s$ are exchangeable: every ordering is equally likely, and $T_0$ takes each of the $s + 1$ ranks with probability $1/(s + 1)$.
:::
